- Queueing model and headroom margins

- KV cache cold-start / warmup behavior and strategies
- Batching windows, token distribution, and p99 tail latency
- Quantization impact on latency and throughput
- VPC / on-prem networking constraints and pinned capacity

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, um we'll run about an hour, go deep on autoscale, i think priya and i will start with the simulation we ran then turn it over, does that work jamal?
[00:00:12] Jamal: yeah that works, thanks alex, we're specifically trying to understand worst case tail behavior when we hit a marketing surge and how reserved pools should be sized. also, we have on-prem considerations — data doesn't leave our VPC so latency to the model matters.
[00:00:26] Priya: high level agenda: queueing headroom math, synthetic burst results, KV cache warmup penalties, then prewarm and eviction policy trade offs. i'll share my screen with the spreadsheet in a sec.
[00:00:38] Marta: quick note, our p99 SLO for the customer flow is 350ms for the first token, if we can't meet that with hosted we need dedicated or private.
[00:00:48] Ethan: and for clarification our token distribution during surge skews longer — avg length 180 tokens but a fat tail.
[00:00:55] Priya: got it, that's helpful — ok loading the burst-sim sheet.
[00:01:12] Priya: (screen) so column A is arrival rate, column B is token length distribution, i'm using an M/M/c-ish approximation with a variance correction because of batching. note this is intentionally conservative on batching efficiency.
[00:01:34] Alex: i just want to flag, real runtime isn't pure M/M/c because of KV cache effects — cold requests can cost 2–6x per-token latency on certain models due to kv reloads. we model that with a two-state service time distribution.
[00:01:52] Jamal: interesting — when you say 'kv reload' is that the remote kv cache resident in RAM on the GPU host, or is that a disk fallback for cold shards?
[00:02:05] Priya: usually it's RAM + host-local nvcache; if the KV entries have been evicted due to pool eviction or long idle, we need to re-populate from the customer model state which adds a startup penalty — we've seen 150–400ms depending on model size and sequence length.
[00:02:24] Marta: so in practice that's going to blow our p99. that's the main concern.
[00:02:30] Priya: yes, so the simulation has two knobs: prewarmed pool size and eviction age threshold. shrinking pools reduces cost but increases the probability of a cold-start at high burst.
[00:02:43] Ethan: can you show the tradeoff curve? like cost vs p99 for different reserved sizes?
[00:02:49] Priya: yep — (scrolling) here's a plot: x axis is reserved GPU count, y left is cost/day, y right is p99 latency. with NimbusFin's traffic trace (I used a synthetic replay based on your emailed histogram) you see diminishing returns after about 6 reserved GPUs for the core traffic pattern; however for a 10x marketing spike you need 12+ to keep p99 below 350ms.
[00:03:18] Jamal: that's huge — 10x is plausible for campaign launches. Is that 12 GPUs in Dedicated mode or in hybrid with prewarmed ephemeral nodes?
[00:03:27] Priya: that's assuming Dedicated pinned GPUs — if you rely on autoscale ephemeral the warmup penalty means you need more prewarmed capacity or you'll see a higher tail. in hybrid you can set a small dedicated baseline (e.g., 4) + autoscale with prewarm pool to smooth bursts.
[00:03:43] Alex: one important note — our autoscaler supports 'soft prewarm' where we keep a small fraction of VMs up with warmed KV caches; they cost less because they have lower concurrency but avoid full cold reload. that's often the sweet spot for marketing spikes.
[00:03:59] Marta: what's the approximate memory overhead for keeping the KV cache warmed per model? we've got a multi-tenant GPU host and memory is the tight constraint.
[00:04:09] Priya: depends on model. for a 30B model the KV cache per active conversation is ~3–4GB. if you keep a warmed instance for a model you need roughly the model + KV, so typically on A100-class it's feasible to have a few warmed instances but not 20 per region.
[00:04:29] Ethan: could quantization reduce KV memory so warming is cheaper?
[00:04:33] Alex: yes, quantization (4-bit or hybrid quant) reduces model footprint and KV storage, which lowers warmup times slightly, but it can also change per-token runtime characteristics — sometimes improving throughput but adding small decoding overhead. we recommend running a short perf bench with your exact prompts.
[00:04:51] Jamal: ok want to examine queueing math — you mentioned a 'variance correction' earlier. what was the assumption?
[00:04:58] Priya: right, typical M/M/c gives mean wait but underestimates tail with batching and variable token lengths. we add a burstiness factor B derived from the coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times and token lengths. effectively service time is S = S_base + S_kvcold*I_cold where I_cold is a Bernoulli for cache miss. we then numerically solve for queue occupancy distribution.
[00:05:20] Marta: how do you determine I_cold probability in production?
[00:05:24] Priya: by measuring idle windows per pooled instance and eviction policies. empirically we've seen cold probability correlate with idle > 90s and pool eviction rates during low traffic windows. if you have 5-minute idle timeouts your cold probability is much lower.
[00:05:38] Ethan: we currently have a 60s idle; is that too aggressive?
[00:05:41] Priya: for your traffic it probably is — with your idle and the marketing spike pattern, cold prob rises to ~0.12 during overlap windows. increasing idle to 300s or having a small dedicated baseline reduces that a lot.
[00:05:54] Alex: another lever is 'KV sticky routing' — route repeat users to the same warmed instance for a TTL window, which helps with conversational workloads. it requires sticky hashing at the router but we've implemented it with fallbacks.
[00:06:08] Jamal: is sticky routing compatible with preemptible instances?
[00:06:11] Priya: partially — if the instance is preempted the router will remap, so you still need fallback capacity. sticky is best combined with a small dedicated pool.
[00:06:21] Marta: what about network egress if we deploy in our on-prem VPC? we saw network adds 10–20ms to RTT to GPUs in a colo.
[00:06:28] Alex: yes network is nontrivial. we recommend colocating inference hosts in your private DC region or using a private peering link. otherwise account for extra latency in the p99 budget — that 10–20ms stacks with KV warmup.
[00:06:40] Ethan: and encryption/KMS for model keys — any perf impact?
[00:06:44] Priya: KMS calls are only during model load and key rotation, not per-token. so warmup can be slightly longer if key fetches happen during scale-up, but not the steady-state per-token path.
[00:06:54] Jamal: ok can we talk about batching windows? our backend can send single request per user but we'd like to tune batching to improve throughput without harming latency.
[00:07:02] Priya: batching window is a microsecond to millisecond tradeoff. for low latency SLOs you'd use a short batching window (e.g., 8–12ms) with small max batch size. if you have bursty arrivals it can improve throughput substantially. our engine supports adaptive batching that expands the window when queue depth is high.
[00:07:20] Alex: important to note batching also changes the effective service time distribution because a batch's service time equals model decode for the longest sequence in the batch plus some overhead. so high variance in token lengths increases tail.
[00:07:32] Marta: any practical rules?
[00:07:34] Priya: yes: limit sequence-length heterogeneity per route (route by median length), use adaptive batching + max batch size of ~16 for 13B-class, and emulate your traffic to tune the window. we can provide the emulation script.
[00:07:48] Ethan: on quantization, you mentioned perf bench. what delta should we expect in p99 if we go to 4-bit from fp16?
[00:07:54] Alex: typically 4-bit quant can reduce latency by 10–25% on decode-heavy workloads and increase throughput 20–40%, but model-specific. also rare failure modes in numerical fidelity can affect output quality — we include eval hooks to detect regressions.
[00:08:10] Jamal: would quant reduce the KV cache rebuild time?
[00:08:14] Priya: modestly — smaller KV footprint means memory moves are quicker, so cold-start time can drop by 10–30% depending on I/O.
[00:08:22] Marta: let's pivot to eviction policy — how do you decide which warmed instances to evict under memory pressure?
[00:08:28] Priya: eviction uses an LRU-ish policy but weighted by recent access frequency and predicted reuse (we have a small ML heuristic). you can prioritize by route importance or customer tier. for NimbusFin we'd recommend tagging high-SLO routes as sticky.
[00:08:44] Alex: we also expose a 'graceful drain' signal so that when an instance is about to be evicted we keep it alive long enough to finish active sessions and optionally snapshot KV to a warm store to speed re-population.
[00:08:58] Ethan: snapshotting KV — that sounds expensive. how long does a snapshot/restore take?
[00:09:03] Priya: for a mid-sized KV (~20M keys) snapshot to local NVMe can be a few hundred ms to a second; restore is similar. it's cheaper than a full rebuild from scratch but not free. that's why warm prewarmed instances are often better for tight p99s.
[00:09:18] Jamal: about the durability of KV state across restarts — is it model-agnostic?
[00:09:22] Priya: KV format is model/architecture dependent but our runtime provides standardized checkpointing so we can persist and restore. there are model-specific optimizations.
[00:09:31] Marta: we want to understand worst-case concurrency. if everyone's marketing surge hits simultaneously how does isolation work across tenants on a multi-tenant host?
[00:09:40] Alex: isolation is twofold: scheduler-level CPU/GPU quotas and soft cgroups; also we provide priority queues where high-tier customers get headroom reservations. you can also get Dedicated capacity for stronger isolation.
[00:09:53] Priya: in simulations we model priority queueing where premium traffic preempts lower-priority batches during resource contention. it's useful if you have mixed-criticality workloads.
[00:10:03] Jamal: ok can you walk through an end-to-end scenario: advertising campaign creates 8x traffic spike for 12 minutes, what's our recommended configuration?
[00:10:12] Priya: scenario: baseline 4 reserved GPUs, 2 prewarm ephemeral instances per region, autoscale up to 16. with that config and adaptive batching we see p99 around 320ms in the sim. if you had only baseline 2 reserved and rely on cold start, p99 jumps to 620ms.
[00:10:30] Marta: can we reduce cost by using preemptible nodes for burst?
[00:10:33] Alex: you can, but preemptible nodes have eviction noise — pair them with reserved baseline and use them to carry non-critical traffic. preemptible are good for lowering marginal cost, not for p99 guarantees.
[00:10:45] Ethan: what telemetry should we stream to detect impending tail increases in real time?
[00:10:50] Priya: key signals: queue depth, fraction of requests hitting cold KV, per-route median sequence length, batch sizes, and instance idle time distribution. also measure p99 decode time separately from network.
[00:11:05] Alex: we can hook into your monitoring via our tracing headers; we also supply Grafana dashboards with alert thresholds.
[00:11:12] Jamal: the dashboard would be helpful. does it show cost per token breakdown?
[00:11:16] Alex: yes token-level cost and where that cost comes from (compute, memory, prewarm).
[00:11:21] Marta: returning to VPC on-prem specifics: if we deploy inside our VPC with private control plane, what differences in autoscaling latencies should we expect?
[00:11:29] Priya: provisioning is generally the same but network bootstrap and KMS calls can add 50–150ms during scale events depending on your KMS latency. also our private build may require longer image pulls if you don't have a local registry.
[00:11:42] Alex: we recommend a small warm reservoir inside the VPC to reduce dynamic pulls.
[00:11:46] Jamal: one more question on pricing — can you provide a cost model for hybrid with reserved baseline + prewarm ephemeral?
[00:11:52] Alex: yes i'll send a pricing sketch; basically reserved covers baseline amortized cost and prewarm ephemeral is priced at a lower per-hour but you pay for instances while they're warmed. we'll include amortized KV warmup and snapshot costs in the model.
[00:12:03] Priya: also note that aggressive quantization reduces steady-state unit cost which changes the cost/performance curve — we'll include a quantization sensitivity tab.
[00:12:12] Jamal: good, let's talk about benchmarks — we want Redwood to run a pass in our environment. what inputs do you need?
[00:12:17] Priya: we need a 7-day traffic trace (timestamps, token counts, route IDs), sample prompts for quality testing, and target SLOs. also which models you want to evaluate and whether quantized variants are allowed.
[00:12:29] Ethan: we'll provide that.
[00:12:31] Priya: great — for on-prem we'll need network topology and available GPU types.
[00:12:36] Marta: we have DGX A100s in colo and some T4s for lower tier workloads.
[00:12:40] Alex: ok good. next steps recap: priya shares the simulation sheet and synthetic scripts; jamal provides traces; alex sends pricing and reserved sizing. we'll schedule a bench week once we get artifacts.
[00:12:52] Jamal: thanks, that sounds good. any final Qs?
[00:12:56] Marta: one tiny thing — for the sticky routing TTL what default would you recommend?
[00:12:59] Priya: 5 minutes is a reasonable starting point for conversational flows, you can tune down for stateless request patterns.
[00:13:07] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and update the CRM.
[00:13:12] Jamal: thanks all.
